messages.author: 4ebc96d60052ef80
messages.subject: Using ggplot2 in undergraduate lectures
parts:
Dear All,

I teach a large first year course in R. There are around 100 students.
Due to the way timetabling works, they haven't covered any other stats
course.

My current schedule is:

~ 3 hours for summary statistics and base R graphics
~ 4 hours for R programming - data types, apply, functions, for loops.
~ 7 hours of other stuff, such as random numbers, monte carlo estimation.

I'm toying with the idea of introducing two hours on ggplot2 lectures
and 2 hours of associated practicals (I would drop something from the
"other stuff").

Is this enough time? Am I being too hopeful to even consider this? My
thoughts are just to use qplot with a few extensions. Does anyone else
teach ggplot to undergraduates (in such a limited time).

Thanks

Colin

--
Dr Colin Gillespie
http://www.mas.ncl.ac.uk/~ncsg3/

messages.author: 17652242ec236632
messages.subject: Re: Using ggplot2 in undergraduate lectures
parts:
Colin,

I teach ggplot2 to a mixed course of undergraduates and graduates. We start using qplot on the first day of class. The students are very quick to pick it up from examples. I provide lots of examples in class using the mpg and diamonds data sets built into ggplot2, and I also have short breakout sessions during the lecture where students can practice using qplot and I can go around to provide individual help.

had.co.nz/ggplot2 also provides many examples for them to get started with. In my experience students can absorb a
lot by starting with a piece of working code and changing it element by element. But we spend much more than two hours on qplot as the course goes very heavily into visualization.

I inherited this class from Hadley and I rely very heavily on his slides and philosophy. So maybe he will have some advice to share. I've seen him teach ggplot2 in a day long workshop (and I've done it myself), so it can be done.Teaching qplot should actually be easier than teaching base R graphics because of the uniform grammar.

Best,
Garrett

parts:
Colin and Garrett,

I was delighted to read this thread since I'm thinking of doing a brief introduction to R and ggplot in a last two meetings of a graduate seminar of quantitative methods. My syllabus (with the last class still under development!) is at http://history.emory.edu/RAVINA/Syllabi/History%20582A.htm

In order to get the most out to two classes, I'm going to skip data manipulation in R -- assuming they will do that in another application -- and focus on the power of simple R commands (boxplot is straightforward!) and the most useful packages: qplot, ggplot, vcd, etc.

I'm appreciate any feedback or advice

Mark

messages.author: 4ebc96d60052ef80
messages.subject: Re: Using ggplot2 in undergraduate lectures
parts:
Hi Hadley, Garrett,

Thanks for your input. I really like the idea of your module, I'm just
not sure if I'll be allowed to teach a module like that - but I will
ask. In your pdf, you mention that it's hard to grade programming - I
completely agree. To a certain extent, it requires 1-to-1 interaction
with the student.

I've developed a few practicals that you might find interesting/useful
(available at http://www.mas.ncl.ac.uk/~ncsg3/teaching/mas1343/pdfs/practicals.pdf)

Practical 2 assessment: Every student gets there own random size
vector and data frame. I ask questions such as "How many values in
your vector are between the mean and median?". Students enter their
answers on a web-form, which I then mark and return individual
"sweaved" results. Good practice for logical operators. Students
haven't encountered "for loops" yet, so they have to work with
vectors.

Practical 3: Students upload some simple functions that I then test
and run. 25% of marks are for code presentation.

Practical 4; Monopoly. Students simulate going round the monopoly
board and estimate the equilibrium distribution of squares they land
on - no money is involved. In the assignment, each question gets
harder. The easiest is, add another Chance card, the most difficult is
if they roll three consecutive doubles, they go to jail. Students
really enjoy this practical - the most popular part of the course!

I can provide the latex/solutions for any of the above.

Cheers

Colin
